claims.source: From these studies, a complex picture has emerged in which ChIs are capable of bi-directionally influencing cell-type specific excitability of both medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and striatal interneurons (Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009) and can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms) (Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneurons can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms).
claims.source: From these studies, a complex picture has emerged in which ChIs are capable of bi-directionally influencing cell-type specific excitability of both medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and striatal interneurons (Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009) and can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms) (Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Acetylcholine release can modulate long term pre and post-synaptic plasticity (minutes to days) on medium spiny projection neurons.
claims.source: Ach release can also modulate long term pre and post-synaptic plasticity (minutes to days) on SPNs (Wang et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Medium spiny projection neurons, interneurons, and dopamine afferents, along with excitatory glutamatergic inputs from thalamus and cortex provide powerful and rapid modulation of the cholinergic interneurons.
claims.source: In turn, SPNs, interneurons, and DA afferents, along with excitatory glutamatergic inputs from thalamus and cortex provide powerful and rapid modulation of the cholinergic interneurons (Aosaki et al., 1994b; Ding et al., 2010; Di Chiara et al., 1994; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Raz et al., 1996; Straub et al., 2014; Witten et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018; Zucca et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Aosaki et al., 1994b; Ding et al., 2010; Di Chiara et al., 1994; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Raz et al., 1996; Straub et al., 2014; Witten et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018; Zucca et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Electrophysiological measurements of naturally occurring cholinergic interneuron signaling in behaving animals have to date been limited to only a few (typically 2–4) putative cholinergic interneurons recorded simultaneously.
claims.source: Electrophysiological measurements of naturally occurring ChI signaling in behaving animals have to date been limited to only a few (typically 2–4) putative ChIs recorded simultaneously and are challenged by difficulties in reliable cell identification.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior studies.

claims.claim: Very little change in cholinergic interneuron population signaling was observed when mice were at rest.
claims.source: Very little change in ChI population signaling was observed when mice were at rest but positive going transients were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement (Figure 1B–C; mean DF/F, p<1e-19 Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: Positive going transients in cholinergic interneuron population signaling were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement.
claims.source: Very little change in ChI population signaling was observed when mice were at rest but positive going transients were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement (Figure 1B–C; mean DF/F, p<1e-19 Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C with statistical significance p<1e-19.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneuron population signals increased rapidly and reliably approximately 100 ms prior to spontaneous movement onsets from rest.
claims.source: ChI population signals increased rapidly and reliably approximately 100 ms prior to spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 1E–F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claims.claim: Very small 'micro' movements occurring at velocities and accelerations below rest threshold did not elicit significant cholinergic interneuron responses.
claims.source: Very small 'micro' movements occurring at velocities and accelerations below our rest threshold did not elicit significant ChI responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Movement onsets from rest could be classified into two types: transitions to continuous locomotion and short duration 'jerks'.
claims.source: Broadly, movement onsets from rest could be classified into two types: transitions to continuous locomotion (Figure 1B,G,K) and short duration 'jerks', consisting of rapidly terminated forward and backward movements (Figure 1B,H,L).
claims.evidence: This is a classification based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Significant elevations in cholinergic interneuron signaling were observed for both locomotion initiations and jerks with similar timing and amplitudes.
claims.source: Significant elevations in ChI signaling were observed for both of these movement onset types with similar timing and amplitudes (Figure 1G,H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claims.claim: A gradual decrease in cholinergic interneuron signal to baseline was observed at locomotion terminations.
claims.source: A gradual decrease in ChI signal to baseline was observed at locomotion terminations (Figure 1B,I,M).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,I,M.

claims.claim: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present in cholinergic interneurons relative to movement onset periods.
claims.source: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present relative to movement onset periods (Figure 1B,D; p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), though transient signaling during these periods was greater than during rest (Figure 1B,D; p<3e-13, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,D with statistical significance p<0.01.

claims.claim: Transient signaling in cholinergic interneurons during continuous locomotion was greater than during rest.
claims.source: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present relative to movement onset periods (Figure 1B,D; p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), though transient signaling during these periods was greater than during rest (Figure 1B,D; p<3e-13, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,D with statistical significance p<3e-13.

claims.claim: The largest cholinergic interneuron transients occurring post-onset were associated with large accelerations at low velocity, corresponding to movement resets in ongoing locomotion.
claims.source: The largest ChI transients (top quartile) occurring post-onset were associated with large accelerations at low velocity, corresponding to movement resets in ongoing locomotion (Figure 1B,J,N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) where the mouse rapidly transitioned to near rest then re-accelerated to resume locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,J,N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Less cholinergic interneuron signal change was associated with accelerations occurring during high velocity, continuous locomotion.
claims.source: Less signal change was associated with accelerations occurring during high velocity, continuous locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneuron movement related signals were observed in the absence of task contingencies, changes in salient sensory stimuli, and before any exposure to rewards.
claims.source: ChI movement related signals were observed in the absence of task contingencies, changes in salient sensory stimuli, and before any exposure to rewards (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H.

claims.claim: Transient dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron population signals reflect rapid transitions in internally generated spontaneous movement, independently of changes in reward prediction or experimentally generated salient stimuli.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that transient dorsal striatum ChI population signals reflect rapid transitions in internally generated spontaneous movement, from rest to movement or during resets in locomotion, independently of changes in reward prediction or experimentally generated salient stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Fiber photometry measures an aggregate weighted average from active cells within a small region (~100–200 µm radius sphere) around the optic fiber.
claims.source: Fiber photometry measures an aggregate weighted average from active cells (cell bodies, axons and dendrites) within a small region (~100–200 µm radius sphere) around the optic fiber (Cui et al., 2013), but single neurons may coordinate in multiple ways to generate the observed population transients (London et al., 2018; Rehani et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the fiber photometry technique, supported by citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral cholinergic interneuron recordings from the same mice.
claims.source: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral recordings from the same mice (Figure 2A), but only dorsal ChI signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Only dorsal cholinergic interneuron signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest.
claims.source: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral recordings from the same mice (Figure 2A), but only dorsal ChI signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Ventral striatum cholinergic interneuron transients did not exhibit consistent timing with respect to spontaneous mouse accelerations.
claims.source: Moreover, unlike dorsal striatum, ventral striatum transients did not exhibit consistent timing with respect to spontaneous mouse accelerations (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Spontaneous movement signals in cholinergic interneurons are different across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similar to dopamine projections.
claims.source: These data indicate that, similar to dopamine projections, spontaneous movement signals in ChIs are different across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2, with comparison to cited dopamine studies.

claims.claim: Delivery of unpredicted water rewards elicited responses in dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons that consisted of a short latency increase followed by a small decrease aligned to the audible solenoid click.
claims.source: Delivery of unpredicted water rewards through a spout near the animals' mouth elicited responses in dorsal striatum ChIs, that on average, consisted of a short latency increase followed by a small decrease aligned to the audible solenoid click associated with water valve opening (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was variable and both the increase and decrease were not reliably present across individual trials.
claims.source: While reminiscent of the previously reported burst/pause observations, this response was variable and both the increase and decrease were not reliably present across individual trials (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Ventral striatum cholinergic interneurons exhibited robust and consistent increases on nearly every trial following reward delivery.
claims.source: In contrast, ventral striatum ChIs exhibited robust and consistent increases on nearly every trial following reward delivery (Figure 2D,I).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,I.

claims.claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was significantly positively correlated with changes in velocity at reward delivery.
claims.source: The dorsal striatum ChI response was significantly positively correlated with these changes in velocity at reward delivery (Figure 2F–H, R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8) but the response in ventral striatum was not (Figure 2J–L, R = −0.17, p=0.06).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H with statistical significance R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8.

claims.claim: The ventral striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was not significantly correlated with changes in velocity at reward delivery.
claims.source: The dorsal striatum ChI response was significantly positively correlated with these changes in velocity at reward delivery (Figure 2F–H, R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8) but the response in ventral striatum was not (Figure 2J–L, R = −0.17, p=0.06).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J–L with statistical result R = −0.17, p=0.06.

claims.claim: Changes in movement at reward consumption could account for much of the dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron population response to unpredicted rewards.
claims.source: These data indicate that dorsal and ventral ChIs exhibit different responses to unpredicted rewards and that changes in movement at reward consumption could account for much of the dorsal striatum ChI population response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A prominent triphasic increase/decrease/increase signal was observed in dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons to a conditioned visual stimulus paired with reward.
claims.source: Notably, we did observe a prominent triphasic increase/decrease/increase signal in dorsal striatum ChIs to a conditioned visual stimulus paired with reward similar to those described in recordings of TANs with electrophysiology (Aosaki et al., 1994a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,G.

claims.claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to conditioned cues could not be fully explained by changes in movement.
claims.source: This response could not be fully explained by changes in movement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G), indicating that dorsal striatum ChIs do display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G.

claims.claim: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
claims.source: This response could not be fully explained by changes in movement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G), indicating that dorsal striatum ChIs do display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G.

claims.claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons exhibited a sustained increase at the conditioned stimulus onset and a sharp increase at the delivery of the predicted reward.
claims.source: Ventral ChIs, in contrast, exhibited a sustained increase at the CS onset and a sharp increase at the delivery of the predicted reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G) consistent with other rodent ventral TAN recordings (Atallah et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claims.claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards but not before.
claims.source: Moreover, ventral ChIs exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards (but not before, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ventral ChIs are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement, a property also present in ventral striatum dopamine signaling (Ko and Wanat, 2016; Syed et al., 2016) and midbrain cell body firing (Coddington and Dudman, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement.
claims.source: Moreover, ventral ChIs exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards (but not before, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ventral ChIs are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement, a property also present in ventral striatum dopamine signaling (Ko and Wanat, 2016; Syed et al., 2016) and midbrain cell body firing (Coddington and Dudman, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, with comparison to cited studies.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneuron signals differ strikingly in their responses to cues, rewards, and to movement across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similarly to dorsal-ventral gradients in dopamine signaling.
claims.source: These findings demonstrate that ChI signals differ strikingly in their responses to cues, rewards, and to movement across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similarly to dorsal-ventral gradients in DA signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Baseline fluorescence in cholinergic interneuron cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing.
claims.source: Since ChIs fire tonically at ~3–10 Hz (Wilson et al., 1990), baseline fluorescence in cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing, while large Ca2+ transients presumably represented bursts of action potentials (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about ChI firing patterns and GCaMP properties, supported by citations to Wilson et al., 1990 and Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Large calcium transients in cholinergic interneurons presumably represented bursts of action potentials.
claims.source: Since ChIs fire tonically at ~3–10 Hz (Wilson et al., 1990), baseline fluorescence in cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing, while large Ca2+ transients presumably represented bursts of action potentials (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about GCaMP properties, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Nearly all single cholinergic interneurons exhibited significantly larger and more frequent calcium transients during all movement periods relative to rest.
claims.source: Consistent with photometry recordings, nearly all single ChIs exhibited significantly larger and more frequent calcium transients during all movement periods relative to rest (Figure 3E, p=4.1e-87 Wilcoxon rank sum test across all cells, 266/268 cells p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance p=4.1e-87.

claims.claim: Single cholinergic interneurons exhibited similar rapid increases to population photometry measures at general movement onsets.
claims.source: Single ChIs exhibited similar rapid increases to population photometry measures at general movement onsets (Figure 3G–H) and increases at jerks and locomotion initiations (Figure 3I–J).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claims.claim: Unlike population photometry measures, transient signaling in single cholinergic interneurons was also prominent during continuous locomotion to a similar extent to locomotion onsets.
claims.source: Unlike the population photometry measures, however, transient signaling in single ChIs was also prominent during continuous locomotion to a similar extent to locomotion onsets (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claims.claim: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light or in mice expressing td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets.
claims.source: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light (rendering GCaMP fluorescence static, that is non-activity dependent) or in separate mice expressing the static red indicator td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single ChIs.
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single cholinergic interneurons.
claims.source: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light (rendering GCaMP fluorescence static, that is non-activity dependent) or in separate mice expressing the static red indicator td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single ChIs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Transient encoding of spontaneous movement is present at movement onsets and during continuous locomotion in the majority of dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons.
claims.source: In summary, transient encoding of spontaneous movement is present at movement onsets and during continuous locomotion in the majority of dorsal striatum ChIs.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Transient synchrony across the population of cholinergic interneurons, rather than signaling amplitude across single cells in the population, may be modulated during behavior.
claims.source: The observation that mean transient changes in dorsal striatum ChI population fluorescence as measured with photometry (Figure 1D), but not single cell transients (Figure 3F), decreased from locomotion initiations to continuous locomotion, raised the possibility that transient synchrony across the population of Chls, rather than signaling amplitude across single cells in the population, may be modulated during behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing data in Figure 1D and Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Synchrony of firing across the cholinergic interneuron network has been identified in vitro as an important determinant of its influence on pre-synaptic dopamine release from axon terminals.
claims.source: Synchrony of firing across the ChI network has been identified in vitro as an important determinant of its influence on pre-synaptic dopamine release from axon terminals (Threlfell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to Threlfell et al., 2012.

claims.claim: High correlations across pairs or triplets of tonically active neurons have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates.
claims.source: High correlations across pairs or triplets of TANs have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates (Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996), but synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of ChIs (>10) during spontaneous movement.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of cholinergic interneurons (>10) during spontaneous movement.
claims.source: High correlations across pairs or triplets of TANs have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates (Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996), but synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of ChIs (>10) during spontaneous movement.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claims.claim: Over all behavior periods, activity across cholinergic interneurons was highly correlated, even for pairs of neurons separated by >400 um.
claims.source: Over all behavior periods, activity across ChIs was highly correlated, even for pairs of neurons separated by >400 um (Figure 4A–E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claims.claim: Transients in cholinergic interneurons were synchronized with a peak at zero phase lag, and this timing was consistent across cell pairs.
claims.source: Transients were synchronized with a peak at zero phase lag, and this timing was consistent across cell pairs (Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claims.claim: Across all behavior periods, there was a weak but significant negative relationship between the magnitude of pairwise correlations and distance between cholinergic interneuron cell pairs separated by distances < 500 um.
claims.source: Also across all behavior periods, there was a weak but significant negative relationship between the magnitude of pairwise correlations and distance between cell pairs separated by distances < 500 um (R = −0.08, p=0.005, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance R = −0.08, p=0.005.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneuron networks are highly synchronized during behavior across large regions of dorsal striatum and positioned to potentially influence dopamine release from local axon terminals.
claims.source: This data indicates that ChI networks are highly synchronized during behavior across large regions of dorsal striatum and positioned to potentially influence dopamine release from local axon terminals.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4, with reference to established mechanisms.

claims.claim: At movement onsets, transients in cholinergic interneurons were highly synchronized.
claims.source: At movement onsets, including both jerks and locomotion initiations, transients were highly synchronized (Figure 4F,H,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and correlations across cell pairs were significantly larger than during rest (p<1e-90, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 4H–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,H,J.

claims.claim: Correlations across cholinergic interneuron cell pairs at movement onsets were significantly larger than during rest.
claims.source: At movement onsets, including both jerks and locomotion initiations, transients were highly synchronized (Figure 4F,H,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and correlations across cell pairs were significantly larger than during rest (p<1e-90, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 4H–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H–I with statistical significance p<1e-90.

claims.claim: At movement onsets, there was a significant negative correlation between cell-cell correlation and anatomical distance in cholinergic interneurons, not present during rest periods.
claims.source: Moreover, there was a significant negative correlation at onsets between cell-cell correlation and anatomical distance, not present during rest periods (p<1e-9, R = −0.26, Figure 4H,J,L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H,J,L with statistical significance p<1e-9, R = −0.26.

claims.claim: Correlations between cholinergic interneuron cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest.
claims.source: Importantly, correlations between cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest (Figure 4G–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but like onsets, there was a strong negative relationship between cell pair correlation and distance (r = −0.42, p<1e-9; Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G–L.

claims.claim: During continuous locomotion, there was a strong negative relationship between cholinergic interneuron cell pair correlation and distance.
claims.source: Importantly, correlations between cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest (Figure 4G–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but like onsets, there was a strong negative relationship between cell pair correlation and distance (r = −0.42, p<1e-9; Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K with statistical significance r = −0.42, p<1e-9.

claims.claim: Synchrony was lower during continuous locomotion despite larger overall mean ΔF/F relative to onsets or rest.
claims.source: Synchrony was lower during continuous locomotion despite larger overall mean DF/F relative to onsets or rest (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 4.

claims.claim: Synchrony and functional spatial organization across cholinergic interneurons is not fixed, but changes with an animal's movement state.
claims.source: These results indicate that synchrony and functional spatial organization across ChIs is not fixed, but changes with an animal's movement state.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The decrease in cholinergic interneuron population transient signaling measured with photometry during continuous running relative to locomotion onset is not likely a result of decreased transient amplitudes in single cholinergic interneurons, but reflects decreased synchrony of transients.
claims.source: The decrease in ChI population transient signaling measured with photometry during continuous running (Figure 1D,E,G) relative to locomotion onset is therefore not likely a result of decreased transient amplitudes in single ChIs (Figure 3F), but reflects decreased synchrony of transients (Figure 4F–K).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claims.claim: Sub-second timescale signals in striatum cholinergic interneuron networks vary with respect to changes in spontaneous movement states.
claims.source: The data presented thus far provides evidence that sub-second timescale signals in striatum Chl networks vary with respect to changes in spontaneous movement states.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claims.claim: Substantia nigra pars compacta cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that SNc cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations and likely influence movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Dopamine signaling likely influences movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that SNc cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations and likely influence movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Signaling in dorsal striatum dopamine axons was highly synchronized across the two hemispheres with zero phase lag.
claims.source: We first established that signaling in dorsal striatum dopamine axons was highly synchronized across the two-hemispheres with zero phase lag (DAT-cre, n = 4; Figure 5A,D,E; mean phase lag DA v DA 0.6 ms, S.E.M 3.5 ms).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D,E.

claims.claim: Cholinergic interneuron population signals were highly synchronized across the two hemispheres of the dorsal striatum with zero phase lag.
claims.source: We then determined that ChI population signals were similarly highly synchronized across the two-hemispheres of the dorsal striatum with zero phase lag (ChAT-cre, n = 6; Figure 5B,F,G; mean phase lag ChI vs ChI 0 ms, S.E.M 5.4 ms).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,F,G.

claims.claim: Dopamine and cholinergic interneuron population transients during locomotion likely reflect general changes in movement state, rather than the kinematics of specific limbs.
claims.source: These new findings indicate that DA and ChI population transients during locomotion likely reflect general changes in movement state, rather than the kinematics of specific limbs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing bilateral synchrony in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Peak cross-correlations between signals from dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons and contralateral dopamine axons was significantly lower than for dopamine/dopamine or cholinergic interneuron/cholinergic interneuron bilateral comparisons.

results.result: The authors establish the background knowledge that cholinergic and dopaminergic neuromodulation in the striatum are crucial for movement control, with prominent models proposing pro-kinetic effects of dopamine and anti-kinetic effects of acetylcholine. However, naturally occurring signaling patterns of cholinergic interneurons during movement and their coordination with dopamine signaling remain unclear.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C38) establish the prior knowledge and gaps in the field through extensive citations to published literature. The authors accurately summarize established findings about cholinergic interneuron function, their role in Parkinson's Disease, and limitations of prior electrophysiology studies. The knowledge claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and provide necessary context for the current study.

results.result: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron population signals increase rapidly (~100 ms prior) at spontaneous movement onsets from rest, including both locomotion initiations and jerks, and are elevated during movement resets, but show reduced transient signaling during continuous high-velocity locomotion compared to movement onsets. These signals occur independently of task contingencies, salient stimuli, or reward exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C51 describe the primary finding that ChI populations signal movement state transitions. The data are supported by fiber photometry recordings with appropriate statistical tests (p<1e-19, p<0.01, p<3e-13) and multiple control conditions (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H). The temporal resolution (~100 ms) and behavioral classifications are clearly defined in methods. Sample sizes (n=19-20 mice, 62 sessions) are adequate.

results.result: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons, but not ventral striatum cholinergic interneurons, rapidly increase signaling at spontaneous movement onsets from rest. Ventral striatum transients do not exhibit consistent timing with spontaneous accelerations, indicating functional differences across the dorsal-ventral axis similar to dopamine projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 demonstrate regional specificity in ChI movement signaling. The comparison is made within the same mice (n=3) using identical recording methods, providing strong internal controls. The findings parallel known dopamine gradients (cited appropriately), strengthening the interpretation. Data are shown in Figure 2A-C with clear differences in timing and amplitude.

results.result: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons show variable responses to unpredicted rewards (short latency increase followed by decrease) that correlate with movement changes at reward delivery (R=0.48, p<1.7e-8), while ventral striatum cholinergic interneurons show robust, consistent increases independent of movement changes (R=-0.17, p=0.06).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 demonstrate differential reward responses across striatal regions. The correlation analysis (C60-C61) appropriately tests whether movement accounts for dorsal ChI responses. The statistical tests are appropriate (Pearson correlation), sample sizes adequate (n=127 dorsal, n=112 ventral rewards), and the p-value for ventral striatum (p=0.06) correctly indicates non-significance. Data are shown in Figure 2D-L.

results.result: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons display a triphasic response to conditioned cues that is partly independent of movement changes, while ventral cholinergic interneurons show sustained increases to conditioned stimuli and sharp increases to predicted rewards. Ventral cholinergic interneurons are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by reward prediction changes coinciding with movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 describe cue and reward prediction responses. The data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) show clear triphasic responses in dorsal striatum and sustained responses in ventral striatum. The conclusion that dorsal responses are 'partly independent' of movement (C64-C65) is appropriately cautious given the correlational analysis. The interpretation about ventral ChI sensitivity to reward prediction (C68) is supported by the before/after reward exposure comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

results.result: Two-photon imaging reveals that nearly all single dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons (266/268 cells) exhibit significantly larger and more frequent calcium transients during movement periods relative to rest (p=4.1e-87). Unlike population photometry, single-cell transient signaling remains prominent during continuous locomotion, similar in extent to locomotion onsets. Movement artifacts cannot account for these transients, as confirmed by control experiments with static fluorophores.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C78 establish single-cell movement encoding. The statistical significance is extremely strong (p=4.1e-87), and nearly all cells (99.3%) show the effect. Critical controls with td-tomato and 800nm excitation (C76-C77, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) rule out movement artifacts. The discrepancy between single-cell and population signals during continuous locomotion (C75) is important for interpreting synchrony results. Sample size (268 neurons, 6 mice) is adequate for cellular imaging.

results.result: Cholinergic interneuron networks show highly synchronized activity across large regions (>400 μm) during behavior, with synchrony significantly elevated at movement onsets (p<1e-90) compared to rest, but significantly reduced during continuous locomotion despite maintained single-cell activity. Synchrony exhibits spatial organization with distance-dependent correlations during movement (R=-0.26 at onsets, R=-0.42 during continuous locomotion, p<1e-9) but not at rest. This dynamic modulation of synchrony, rather than single-cell amplitude changes, accounts for the reduced population photometry signal during continuous locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C94 present a major finding about dynamic network synchrony. The statistical evidence is strong (p<1e-90 for onset vs rest comparison, p<1e-9 for distance correlations). The analysis appropriately uses cross-correlations and distance-dependent measures. The conclusion that synchrony, not amplitude, drives population signals (C94) is well-supported by comparing Figures 1D, 3F, and 4F-K. Sample size (up to 15 cells simultaneously, 1060 cell pairs, 6 mice) is substantial for 2-photon imaging. The zero-phase-lag synchrony (C84) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Sub-second timescale signals in striatum cholinergic interneuron networks vary with spontaneous movement states. Previous work has established that dopamine signals also fluctuate rapidly with spontaneous locomotor changes and likely influence movement drive on sub-second timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide a transition summary and cite established dopamine findings appropriately (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016). C95 accurately summarizes the current findings from Figures 1-4. The citations for dopamine findings (C96-C97) are appropriate and set up the rationale for simultaneous recordings.

results.result: A novel bilateral fiber photometry approach reveals that dopamine axon signals and cholinergic interneuron population signals are each highly synchronized across hemispheres with zero phase lag, but dopamine/cholinergic cross-correlations are significantly lower (p<1e-10) and show significant phase offsets (mean peak lag +114 ms, mean trough lag -180 ms). These timing differences cannot be attributed to calcium dynamics differences or axon transmission delays, as confirmed by control experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C109 establish a new technical approach and reveal temporal coordination between DA and ChI signals. The bilateral synchrony findings (C98-C99) validate the approach. The phase offset measurements (C102) are precise and consistent. Critical controls address alternative explanations: subcellular compartment calcium dynamics (C104, Figure 5M), axon transmission delays (C105-C106, Figure 5L-M), and contralateral projections (C107-C108, Figure 5N-O). Sample sizes are adequate (n=4 DAT-cre, n=6 ChAT-cre, n=8 DAT/ChAT-cre mice). The statistical significance (p<1e-10) is strong.

results.result: Both dopamine axons and cholinergic interneurons show stronger transient signaling during movement than rest (p<1e-6) and correlate with acceleration and velocity but with different timing. Dopamine signals increase at movement onsets (p<0.01) but show elevated signaling during continuous locomotion relative to onsets (p<0.01), while cholinergic interneurons show the opposite pattern. This indicates both systems respond to movement changes but may contribute differently to distinct movement states.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 compare DA and ChI dynamics during different movement phases. The statistical tests are appropriate (Wilcoxon rank-sum) with significant p-values. The finding that DA signals are elevated during continuous locomotion while ChI signals decrease (C114 vs C46) is a key difference. Sample size (n=8 mice, 25 recordings) is adequate. The data are from mice without reward exposure, controlling for reward-related confounds. The conclusion about differential contributions (C115) is appropriately cautious ('may not be equivalent').

results.result: At locomotion initiations, both dopamine and cholinergic interneurons increase rapidly (dopamine slightly lagging), but at jerk onsets, dopamine signals decrease below baseline while cholinergic interneurons increase similarly to locomotion initiations. Cholinergic transients at rest strongly predict movement transitions and are associated with larger velocity increases when accompanied by large dopamine signals, while dopamine transients alone are only weakly predictive of movement transitions. This suggests cholinergic synchrony signals movement state transitions while dopamine signals whether movements are facilitated or terminated.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C124 present a major mechanistic finding about DA/ChI coordination at movement onsets. The differential responses at locomotion initiations vs jerks (C116-C117, Figure 6G-J) are clearly demonstrated. The predictive analysis (C118-C121, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) appropriately tests causal relationships. The finding that ChI transients predict movement but DA transients alone do not (C120-C121) is important. Sample sizes are adequate (n=94 locomotion initiations, n=292 jerks, 8 mice). The proposed model (C123-C124) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: During continuous locomotion, dopamine and cholinergic interneuron signals show strong negative correlation, with dopamine positively correlated with velocity at near-zero phase lag while cholinergic interneurons show negative correlation at positive lags. Velocity increases are associated with dopamine increases followed by cholinergic desynchronization, while velocity decreases are associated with dopamine decreases followed by cholinergic synchrony increases. Synchronous cholinergic transients during continuous locomotion are associated with velocity decreases when not accompanied by strong dopamine signals, but with velocity increases ('resets') when both signals occur together.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C138 describe complex DA/ChI dynamics during continuous locomotion. The negative correlation (C126, Figure 7A-C) contrasts with positive correlation at initiations (C125). The differential velocity correlations (C128-C129, Figure 7E) are clearly shown. The analysis of velocity increases/decreases (C130-C131, Figure 7F-H) appropriately tests the proposed relationships. The finding that ChI transients predict different outcomes depending on DA signals (C132-C133, Figure 7I-J) is important. The proposed model (C138) integrates the findings coherently. Sample sizes are adequate (n=18 recordings for continuous locomotion, 8 mice).

results.result: The authors propose a new model where synchronous cholinergic interneuron network activations support rapid reconfigurations in the striatum network that facilitate internally triggered changes in movement state, and dopamine and acetylcholine act both synergistically and competitively to regulate different aspects of movement depending on behavioral state.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 present the overarching model integrating all findings. C139 is explicitly labeled as a hypothesis, which is appropriate. The model is well-supported by the extensive data on: (1) ChI synchrony at state transitions (C4-C6, C87-C94), (2) differential DA/ChI dynamics across movement types (C116-C117, C125-C138), and (3) predictive relationships (C118-C124). The conclusion that DA and ACh act both synergistically and competitively (C140) is supported by the finding of positive correlation at initiations but negative correlation during continuous locomotion (C125-C126). The model represents a significant conceptual advance.

results.result: Viral expression specificity was validated by immunohistochemistry, showing that 97.3% (SD 2.3%) of GCaMP6f-expressing neurons in dorsal striatum and 98.3% (SD 1.5%) in ventral striatum co-expressed ChAT, confirming selective labeling of cholinergic interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 provide essential validation of cell-type specificity. The quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) shows high specificity (>97%) with low variability across three mice. Sample sizes for cell counts are adequate (n=100, 69, 50 cells in dorsal striatum; n=68, 33, 46 in ventral striatum). This validation is critical for interpreting all ChI-related findings and rules out contamination from other cell types. The immunohistochemistry approach (ChAT antibody) is appropriate.

results.result: Fiber photometry measures an aggregate weighted average from active cells within a small region (~100-200 μm radius sphere) around the optic fiber, but single neurons may coordinate in multiple ways to generate observed population transients.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 accurately describes the technical limitations of fiber photometry, appropriately citing Cui et al., 2013. This methodological consideration is important for interpreting the discrepancy between population and single-cell signals and motivates the 2-photon imaging experiments. The statement is appropriately cautious about interpretation.
